name: Nudge
description: Choice architecture -- how options are structured, defaulted, or framed -- can shift behavior without restricting choice or changing economic incentives. Overall effect sizes reported in the literature range from small-to-medium to functionally near-zero depending on how publication bias is corrected for, and effectiveness varies widely by intervention type and context.
design_relevance_note: The umbrella justification behind default options, opt-out enrollment, and choice-structure changes generally -- but this corpus's own evidence trail is the clearest argument in the whole taxonomy for treating any single 'nudge' claim skeptically until its specific intervention type and context are checked, rather than assuming the category as a whole is reliably effective.
myth_risk_note: This is close to the textbook case this taxonomy's myth_risk field was built for: 'nudge' is maximally prevalent (it names the field), routinely cited as reliably effective in popular and trade-book discourse, and this corpus's own bias-corrected reanalysis of the leading meta-analysis found the effect largely disappears for two of three intervention categories. High risk that a design decision citing 'nudge theory' in general, without specifying intervention type, is citing something considerably weaker than assumed.
prevalence_note: Arguably the single most foundational term in this entire corpus's subject area -- the word 'nudge' itself names the behavioral-design discipline this graph exists to hold accountable.

findings.description: Across 317 effect sizes from 100 primary publications, nudge effectiveness varies widely by intervention type and context; some nudges are ineffective or backfire; digital and non-digital nudging compared directly.
findings.source_title: How effective is nudging? A quantitative review on the effect sizes and limits of empirical nudging studies
findings.source_venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics

findings.description: Choice architecture interventions overall promote behavior change with a small-to-medium effect (Cohen's d = 0.45, 95% CI [0.39, 0.52]); decision-structure interventions consistently outperform decision-information or decision-assistance interventions; food-choice domain shows effects up to 2.5x larger than other domains.
findings.source_title: The effectiveness of nudging: A meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions across behavioral domains
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

findings.description: Once Mertens et al.'s own dataset is re-analyzed with bias-correction (robust Bayesian meta-analysis), the combined effect drops to approximately d = 0.04 (BF01 = 0.95) — evidence against an effect in the 'information' and 'assistance' intervention categories; evidence for 'structure' interventions remains undecided rather than disproven.
findings.source_title: No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

applications.title: HMRC's 'nine out of ten people pay their tax on time' letters raised debt repayment by 15 percentage points
applications.description: The UK's HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) Debt Management and Banking Team partnered with the Behavioural Insights Team to test social-norm messaging in tax-debt reminder letters. In an initial trial sent to 140,000 taxpayers, a control letter (no social norm) was compared against letters stating '9 out of 10 people in Britain pay their tax on time', with some variants also citing the recipient's own postcode or town. Response rates after three months rose from 67.5% (control) to 72.5% (national norm), 79.0% (postcode norm), and 83.0% (town norm). A separate, more tightly controlled RCT on 1,400 late payers with about GBP4 million in total debt isolated the effect of a localised norm message alone: payment rates rose from 38.7% to 45.5%, a 15-percentage-point increase, holding the rest of the letter's wording identical to the control. HMRC's own published estimate: if rolled out nationally, this effect could advance approximately GBP160 million of tax debt to the Exchequer over a six-week period.
applications.industry_context: UK central government tax administration and debt collection.
applications.ethical_note: The message itself is truthful (the cited compliance statistic is real, not fabricated) and the underlying goal -- collecting money already legally owed, to fund public services -- is legitimate, unlike many dark-pattern uses of social proof. But this specific application targets people already in a vulnerable position (tax debtors, some already behind on payments) with a social-comparison message designed to apply psychological pressure toward compliance, rather than addressing why they fell behind -- a genuinely mixed case, not a clean user-beneficial one.
